children.html: Practice Variability and Transfer of Training: The Role of Self-Efficacy Generality
Miguel A. Quin˜ones University of Arizona

Practice variability has been shown to enhance transfer of training. The purpose of the present study was to examine the role of self-efficacy generality as a motivational mechanism in explaining the relationship between practice variability and transfer. Undergraduate students (N 82) were randomly assigned to 1 of 2 training conditions (constant or variable) for a computer decision-making task. Measures of self-efficacy (intensity and generality) and transfer (near and far) were assessed. The results provided support for some of the hypothesized relationships. Specifically, practice variability led to increased self-efficacy generality. Both self-efficacy intensity and generality influenced far transfer performance, although only self-efficacy generality served as a mediator between practice variability and far transfer.

The ultimate goal of training is to enhance the knowledge, skills, and abilities of an individual, which will lead to an increase in performance in the work setting. To that end, researchers have tried to identify variables that enhance the transfer of training (Ghodsian, Bjork, & Benjamin, 1997; Goldstein, 1993). Specifically, past research has manipulated the scheduling (random or blocked) or the type (variable or constant) of practice (e.g., Kerr & Booth, 1978; Shea & Morgan, 1979) in order to increase transfer performance. More recently researchers have combined these two practice features to optimize transfer (Hall & Magill, 1995; Lee, Magill, & Weeks, 1985). Although there have been inconsistent findings suggesting that the combination of random variable practice leads to a detrimental training performance, the findings indicating that random variable practice leads to an enhanced transfer performance have been more persuasive (Schmidt & Bjork, 1992).

The importance of introducing variability during training so that individuals do not rely on a specific set of responses that will ultimately reduce their chances for transfer and generalization of skills has been stressed in the literature (Kadzin, 1975; Shute & Gawlick, 1995). Past research examining the relative advantage of practice variability has typically taken a cognitive approach (e.g., Baldwin & Ford, 1988; Holding, 1991; McGehee & Thayer, 1961; Schmidt, 1975; Thorndike & Woodworth, 1901). Self-efficacy refers to "the judgments of one's capability to organize and execute the courses of action required to produce given attainments" (Bandura, 1997, p. 3). Self-efficacy has been proposed to vary along three dimensions: level, strength, and generality. First, people may differ in the difficulty of tasks that they believe they are capable in performing (level). Second, individuals may differ in their confidence in attaining a given level of performance (strength). Finally, efficacy beliefs associated with one activity can be generalized to similar ones within the same activity domain or across a range of activities (generality).

Most studies have typically focused on two dimensions of self-efficacy, level and strength. These studies have shown that successful performances increase self-efficacy level and strength (Bandura, 1982, 1991; Gist, 1986, 1989; Martocchio & Judge, 1997; Mitchell, Hopper, Daniels, George-Falvy, & James, 1994; Shea & Howell, 2000), that higher self-efficacy level leads to more constructive interpretations and attributions of behavioral outcomes (e.g., Gist & Mitchell, 1992; Martocchio & Webster, 1992), and that higher self-efficacy strength leads to more successful performance outcomes (e.g., Bandura & Cervone, 1986; Schunk, 1991; Ford, Smith, Weissbein, Gully, & Salas, 1998). These findings indicate that the two dimensions have similar antecedents and consequences; however, this is not surprising given research showing that the two dimensions overlap (e.g., Cecil & Pinkerton, 2000), and as a result, they would be expected to behave similarly.
However, to date, few studies have empirically examined selfefficacy generality. Individuals who demonstrate high self-efficacy

generality are expected to have similar ratings of self-efficacy level and strength across a variety of tasks. If these tasks are very similar, generality is said to be specific. If the tasks are different but are within the same domain of tasks, generality is said to be intermediate. Global generality occurs when the tasks are different and span across various domains (Bandura, 1997). Past research (e.g., Bong, 1997) has investigated the intermediate level of generality and has shown that self-efficacy beliefs for a particular class of performances are related (e.g., academic self-efficacy). The present research looks at the specific level of generality where it is expected that self-efficacy ratings for one version of the training task will generalize to other versions of the same task. Namely, individuals with high generality will have highly related (i.e., similar) efficacy ratings within a training task. It is predicted that this dimension of self-efficacy is not redundant with level and strength, and as such, may not behave in the same manner to similar antecedents or result in the same consequences.

Practice variability is likely to result in inconsistent performance as trainees attempt to master a task with changing characteristics or elements. Successes are also likely to be accompanied with failure and result in highly variable performance during training. In fact, past research has demonstrated that individuals trained under a variable practice regimen tend to perform relatively poorly during training (cf. Schmidt & Bjork, 1992). By comparison, those trained under a constant practice condition are likely to experience steadily increasing levels of performance as they quickly learn the task.
Hypothesis 1a: Practice variability will be positively related to training performance variability.
Hypothesis 1b: Practice variability will be negatively related to training performance level.

The level of performance experienced during training is likely to influence trainees' judgments of their capacity to perform similar tasks in the future (self-efficacy). In accordance, because selfefficacy is derived from past experience with similar tasks (Pajares & Miller, 1995; Woodruff & Cashman, 1993), we propose that past experience in the form of performance variability will influence the dimensions of self-efficacy. Specifically, low performance variability accompanied by steadily increasing performance level (i.e., low practice variability trainees) should lead to an increased self-efficacy level, because the perceived difficulty of the task is lowered, and strength, because confidence for the particular task is raised. By contrast, high performance variability will dampen trainees' overall self-efficacy judgments because they are not performing the task consistently well. However, because they are experiencing a broader range of the task, their selfefficacy judgments are likely to be relatively constant across different versions of the task (higher generality). On the other hand, constant practice trainees' higher self-efficacy judgments are likely to be limited to a narrow range of the task (low generality).
Hypothesis 2a: Practice variability will be positively related to self-efficacy generality.
Hypothesis 2b: Practice variability will be negatively related to self-efficacy level and strength.

It has been argued that practice variability will lead to differences in the experienced success and failure of trainees. These experiences drive trainees' judgments of their future success and failure on the task (self-efficacy).
Hypothesis 3a: Performance variability will mediate the relationship between practice variability and self-efficacy generality.
Hypothesis 3b: Performance variability will mediate the relationship between practice variability and self-efficacy level and strength.

Transfer can be separated into two subcategories: (a) near transfer, in which the stimulus in the transfer condition is similar to the stimulus in the original learning condition and (b) far transfer, in which the stimulus in the transfer condition is to some degree different from the stimulus in the original learning condition (Royer, 1979). It is proposed that different dimensions of selfefficacy are necessary to explain the occurrences of these two subcategories of transfer.

That is, we expect self-efficacy level, strength, and generality to be related to a particular subcategory of transfer performance. Although the dimensions' relationships with near and far transfer are different, the basis for the two predicted relationships is the same: People's estimates of their capabilities influence which tasks they choose to perform, the effort they choose to expend, and the persistence they choose to exert (Woodruff & Cashman, 1993). Thus, estimates, which are based on the perceived difficulty of (level) and confidence for (strength) a trained task, will be related to performance on an identical transfer task (near transfer). In fact, a number of studies have found a positive relationship between self-efficacy level and strength with training performance and near transfer (Eden & Aviram, 1993; Gist, Stevens, & Bavetta, 1991; Martocchio, 1994; Mathieu, Martineau, & Tannebaum, 1993; Mitchell et al., 1994; Stevens & Gist, 1997). Furthermore, estimates, which are based on experience with a range of stimuli within a task (generality), will be related to performance on transfer tasks differing from the original learning condition (far transfer). That is, people with higher generality will have greater estimates of their capabilities for a broader range of tasks including those that have not been practiced. As a result, individuals with higher self-efficacy generality should perform better on far transfer tasks.
Hypothesis 4a: Self-efficacy level and strength will be positively related to near transfer performance.
Hypothesis 4b: Self-efficacy generality will be positively related to far transfer performance.

The hypotheses presented thus far suggest that practice variability influences self-efficacy, which in turn, influences transfer. In fact, others have suggested that self-efficacy may be "an intervening variable between training and task performance" (Gist, 1989,

p. 803). Gist (1986) found support for this statement, and as such, designing training to boost self-efficacy has been investigated as a means to increase later transfer performance. However, the present study suggests that the different dimensions of self-efficacy may mediate different aspects of transfer performance.
Hypothesis 5a: Self-efficacy level and strength will mediate the relationship between practice variability and near transfer performance.
Hypothesis 5b: Self-efficacy generality will mediate the relationship between practice variability and far transfer performance.

A computer naval air defense simulation presented on a PC-compatible microcomputer was used as the task for this experiment. In this simulation, 82 undergraduate students (36 men, 46 women) commanded a U.S. naval vessel and made decisions regarding a series of targets (Hollenbeck et al., 1997; Quin˜ones, 1995). Specifically, the values of the nine attributes as well as the three interactions among six of the nine attributes helped to determine the level of threat, from non- to somewhat to very threatening of the target (for more detail see Hollenbeck et al., 1997). The participant was asked to take a defensive position (ignore, monitor, warn, ready, defend) depending on these nine target attributes within an allotted amount of time. The individual was then given feedback as to the accuracy of his or her judgment and was awarded points accordingly. That is, the number of points awarded depended on the distance between the individual's decision and the correct decision, which resulted in five possible outcomes for each trial: hit (2 points), near miss (1 point), miss (0 points), incident (-1 point), and disaster (-2 points). For example, the participant received a "near miss" if the participant's decision (e.g., ignore) was one level away from the correct decision (e.g., monitor).

In this study, practice variability was operationalized as the number of target attributes (of nine) that changed in value from one trial to the next. Although some of the attributes were randomly assigned a value by the computer (i.e., these attributes were changing), the other attributes were held at a fixed value in the "somewhat threatening" range. Using this method of manipulating practice variability, two practice conditions were created.

Constant practice condition. In this condition, the number of attributes assigned random values by the computer remained the same throughout the practice session. Specifically, in this condition, three of the nine attributes changed in value. Thus, it was important for the participants to focus on those three attributes that changed and their relation to the other six attributes. That is, the specific set of attributes being assigned values by the computer changed; however, all the trials for a specific set of attributes were practiced before beginning trials with the other sets of attributes (blocked scheduling).

Variable practice condition. In this practice condition, the number of attributes (either three or six) assigned random values by the computer varied throughout the practice session. More specifically, the set of attributes was practiced in a random order such that the same set of attributes was never practiced in two sequential trials. Further, the trials with sets of three attributes assigned values by the computer were interspersed with the trials with sets of six attributes assigned values by the computer.
Although the number of attributes changing in value was dependent on the practice condition, the difficulty was expected to be comparable for the
two conditions because all nine attributes were to be measured by participants and contributed to the overall threat of the target.

Self-efficacy. In the self-efficacy measure, participants indicated whether they could achieve a specific number of points in the air defense task and what their level of confidence (0% to 100%) was in achieving these points (strength). Participants were also asked to indicate the exact number of points that they could achieve (level). Participants made these ratings for nine different variations of the air defense task, ranging from one target attribute changing all the way up to all nine target attributes changing. From this measure, the three dimensions of self-efficacy were operationalized in multiple ways in order to examine the relationship among the various measures (Maurer & Pierce, 1998).

Self-efficacy level was computed by averaging the number of points participants indicated when asked to predict how many points they could achieve for each of the nine variations of the task. Self-efficacy level was also computed by taking the maximum number of points indicated by a participant across the nine variations of the task.

Self-efficacy strength was the mean of confidence ratings (0% no confidence, 100% high confidence) for achieving various levels of points during a session for the nine versions of the task. A second measure of self-efficacy strength was computed by taking the maximum confidence level across all versions of the task.

As discussed previously, generality is determined by the similarity of self-efficacy (level and strength) ratings across different task versions. Because of the scarcity of research on this dimension, self-efficacy generality was assessed by two methods. First, to descriptively examine self-efficacy generality (a) the factor structures of level and strength were examined, (b) the intercorrelations among the self-efficacy level and strength ratings for the nine versions of the task were also examined, and (c) the pattern of the self-efficacy level and strength ratings for the nine versions were explored. Second, a measure of self-efficacy generality was created using an inferential method similar to Bong (1997). Specifically, two measures of generality were computed by taking the variance of both the level scores and the strength scores across the nine task versions. When a participant indicated similar self-efficacy level or strength values across all versions of the task, a small variance resulted. A small variance was indicative of a broader generalization meaning that the participant held similar efficacy beliefs across the different versions of the task (high generality). However, when a participant indicated a high self-efficacy level or strength value for one version of the task but indicated low self-efficacy level or strength values for the other versions of the task (i.e., the person had differing efficacy beliefs for the different versions of the task), a high variance resulted. Thus, a high variance was indicative of a narrower generalization (low generality). These two measures were reverse scored and then rezeroed for ease of interpretability so that higher scores indicated higher generality.

Training performance. The number of points for a trial was based on the accuracy of the judgments made. Participants' training performance was broken down into four blocks of 12 trials in order to evaluate the training performance of the two training conditions over time. The mean and variance of the points attained for each of the four blocks were computed.

Transfer performance. The number of points for a trial was based on the accuracy of the judgments made, just as in the training performance measure. Participants' transfer performance was assessed by (a) near transfer (the mean number of points attained on those 10 trials identical to those practiced during training; three attributes changing) and (b) far transfer (the mean number of points attained on those 20 trials that had not been previously practiced in training; five and eight attributes changing).

Individual differences. Because this research is still in a preliminary stage, the present study was interested in isolating the effect of self-efficacy in the relationship between practice variability and transfer. As such,

individual differences that have been previously shown to be related to training and transfer performance were measured and included in all analyses as covariates. Specifically, participants were given a two-factor measure of goal orientation (Roedel, Schraw, & Plake, 1994). The items, rated on a Likert-type scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree), assessed both learning (e.g., "I work hard even when I don't like a class"; 12 items; .70) and performance (e.g., "It is important to me to always do better than others"; 5 items, .75) orientations. As learning goal orientation has been shown to influence both performance (Fisher & Ford, 1998; Ford et al., 1998) and self-efficacy (Kozlowski et al., 2001; Steele-Johnson, Beauregard, Hoover, & Schmidt, 2000; Towler & Dipboye, 2001), it was necessary to look at the effect of self-efficacy taking into account the participants' learning goal orientation. Furthermore, although research regarding the effect of performance orientation on performance (Fisher & Ford, 1998; Hoffman, 1993) and selfefficacy (Chen, Gully, Whiteman, & Kilcullen, 2000; Bell & Kozlowski, 2002; Phillips & Gully, 1997) has been less consistent, finding no relationship or sometimes a negative relationship, it was also necessary to take into account any effects performance orientation may have had on the relationships of interest.

In addition, a measure of general cognitive ability (Wonderlic, 1992) was administered to participants. Byrnes (1995) argued for the control of cognitive ability in situations in which "the speed of information processing could affect performance" (p. 7). As the task in this experiment was in fact limited in time, the use of general cognitive ability as a covariate allowed for the controlled consideration of the influence of training on the participants' performance.

Participants were given a brief introduction to the experiment during which time they were given premeasures to assess their goal orientation and general cognitive ability. Following the completion of these measures, the participants were given a packet with a description of the rules for the air defense task. They were told that a certain number of attributes would be changing, whereas the other attributes would remain at fixed values, but they should measure all nine attributes because they would not know which attributes would change in value. Further, they were told that their scores were reflective of the accuracy with which they judged each target.

The participants were randomly assigned to one of the two experimental conditions (constant vs. variable practice). Participants in the constant practice condition received training on three attributes changing, six attributes fixed. Participants in the variable practice condition received

training on both (a) three attributes changing, six attributes fixed and (b) six attributes changing, three attributes fixed. Participants in both conditions practiced the computer task for a total of 48 trials. Following the training session, participants were given the task self-efficacy measure. After completion of the self-efficacy measure, the participants were tested on a transfer task (30 trials: 10 near and 20 far) in which the feedback received was the same as that received during training.

In the present study, repeated measures analyses were conducted for Hypotheses 1a and 1b, and hierarchical regressions were conducted for Hypotheses 2a–5b. Individual differences (i.e., general cognitive ability, learning orientation, performance orientation) were not of interest in the present study. Therefore, to control for any effect they may have had, they were used as covariates in all the analyses. Furthermore, in the regression analyses, to test the relationships of interest, additional variables were controlled (e.g., to examine the relationship between self-efficacy and transfer, practice variability was controlled). The steps in each hierarchical regression are detailed in the individual table for the corresponding hypothesis.

Before testing the present study's hypotheses, we wanted to look at the overall effect of practice variability on performance. Therefore, a repeated measures analysis was conducted with type of performance (training, near, far) as a within-subjects variable and training condition as the between-subjects variable. The multivariate type-by-condition interaction was significant, Pillai's Trace .133, F(2, 76) 5.82, p .01, -2 .133. Figure 1 shows that the variable condition had lower training performance than transfer performance (performance was similar for near and far transfer measures). By contrast, the constant practice group had much lower far transfer performance relative to training and near transfer performance.
Figure 1. The interaction between training condition and type of performance on performance level.

Hypothesis 1 (a and b) stated that individuals in the variable condition would have greater performance variability and lower performance mean levels than would individuals in the constant condition. To test this hypothesis, two repeated measures analyses were conducted with time (Block 1, Block 2, Block 3, Block 4) as the within-subjects variable and training condition as the betweensubjects variable. For training performance variability, the multivariate time-by-condition interaction was nonsignificant, Pillai's Trace = .075, F(3, 75) = 2.02, p > .05, \eta^2 = .075. However, there was an effect of training condition, F(1,77) = 8.20, p < .01, \eta^2 = .096, showing that the variable condition had greater training performance variability than the constant condition at each training block. For training performance mean, the multivariate time-bycondition interaction was significant, Pillai's Trace = .235, F(3,75) = 7.68, p < .01, \eta^2 = .235. Over time, the training performance level (M) of the constant condition continually increased, whereas the variable condition decreased at Block 4. These results fully support Hypothesis 1 (a and b). For ease of interpretability, two composite measures, training performance mean and training performance variability, were formed from the four training blocks for use in future analyses. Specifically, the composite for training performance mean was used as a covariate in analyses of transfer (Hypotheses 4a-5b) in order to account for differences in acquisition and, therefore, better isolate the effects of practice variability. The composite for training performance variability was used in the analyses of self-efficacy (Hypotheses 2a-3b) to test for its possible mediating effect.

Hypothesis 2a predicted that individuals in the variable condition would have higher self-efficacy generality than individuals in the constant condition. This hypothesis was examined by descriptive and inferential tests to determine the similarity of self-efficacy (level and strength) ratings across different task versions, that is, generality. First, two principal components factor analyses with a varimax rotation for the nine self-efficacy level ratings and nine self-efficacy strength ratings were conducted by condition to examine the respective factor structures. For the variable condition, the factor analysis resulted in a one-factor structure for level (eigen value = 7.81; %variance = 86.76) and a one-factor structure for strength (eigen value = 7.66; %variance = 85.08). For the constant condition, the factor analysis resulted in a two-factor structure for level (eigen value<sub>1</sub> = 4.51; eigen value<sub>2</sub> = 4.07; % variance = 95.32) and a two-factor structure for strength (eigen value_1 = 4.36; eigen value_2 = 4.30; % variance = 96.28). Second, the intercorrelations for both level and strength ratings were examined to determine their similarity by condition. The average correlation among the nine self-efficacy level ratings for the variable condition (M = .83, SD = .13) was slightly higher than the average correlation for the constant condition (M = .81, SD =.14), although not statistically significant, t(78) = .55, p > .05. However, the average correlation among the nine self-efficacy strength ratings for the variable condition (M = .85, SD = .11) was higher than the average correlation for the constant condition (M =.74, SD = .20), t(77) = 4.18, p < .01. Third, to examine the pattern of self-efficacy ratings, two repeated measures analyses were conducted with self-efficacy ratings (1-9) as a withinsubjects variable and training condition as the between-subjects

variable. For self-efficacy level, the multivariate self-efficacy ratings-by-condition interaction was significant, Pillai's Trace = .210, F(8, 67) = 2.22, p = .04, \eta^2 = .210. As a result, the pattern of self-efficacy levels was flatter for the variable condition than for the constant condition. In fact, the difference between the highest and lowest ratings of self-efficacy level was smaller for the variable condition (6.25/20) than the constant condition (8.62/20). For self-efficacy strength, the multivariate self-efficacy ratings-bycondition interaction was significant, Pillai's Trace = .216, F(8,(68) = 2.34, p = .03, \eta^2 = .216. Again, the pattern of self-efficacy strengths was flatter for the variable condition than for the constant condition. That is, the difference between the highest and lowest ratings of self-efficacy strength was smaller for the variable condition (196.14/700) than for the constant condition (269.14/700). These findings indicate that the variable condition had more similar self-efficacy level ratings and more similar self-efficacy strength ratings across different task versions than the constant condition. The more similar ratings descriptively provide evidence for higher generality in the variable condition.

As discussed in the Method section, the measures of selfefficacy (i.e., mean, maximum, and variance of self-efficacy level and strength ratings) were formed. These six measures were factor analyzed using a principal components factor analysis with a varimax rotation. The first factor, termed self-efficacy intensity, consisted of the four measures intended to capture the two selfefficacy dimensions of level and strength: the mean of selfefficacy level, the mean of self-efficacy strength, the maximum of self-efficacy level, and the maximum of self-efficacy strength (eigen value = 3.31; standardized \alpha = .93). The second factor, self-efficacy generality, consisted of the two measures meant to assess this dimension of self-efficacy: variance of self-efficacy level and variance of self-efficacy strength (eigen value = 1.87; standardized \alpha = .82). These two factors accounted for 86.26% of the variance and were unrelated (r = -.08, p > .05; see Table 1). Because the six measures were on different scales, they were standardized before they were summed into their respective composite measures. All further analyses were conducted on these composites.

In the final test of Hypothesis 2a, the regression analysis showed that practice variability had a significant effect on self-efficacy generality (\beta = .295, p = .01; see Table 2). As a result, individuals in the variable condition (M = 9.70, SD = 1.83) had higher self-efficacy generality than individuals in the constant condition (M = 8.66, SD = 1.83). Thus, Hypothesis 2a was fully supported by the findings from each of the above (descriptive and inferential) tests.

Hypothesis 2b stated that individuals in the constant condition (low practice variability) would have higher self-efficacy intensity than individuals in the variable condition. The regression analyses revealed that practice variability had no significant effect on self-efficacy intensity (\beta = .194, p > .05; see Table 2). As such, Hypothesis 2b was not supported.

Hypotheses 3a and 3b stated that training performance variability would mediate the relationship between practice variability and self-efficacy generality and between practice variability and self-efficacy intensity, respectively. As shown in Table 3, training performance variability had no effect on self-efficacy generality (\beta = -.036, p > .05) or self-efficacy intensity (\beta = -.144, p > .05). Thus, Hypotheses 3a and 3b were not supported.

We predicted that self-efficacy intensity would be positively related to near transfer performance (Hypothesis 4a) and that self-efficacy generality would be positively related to far transfer performance (Hypothesis 4b). As shown in the regression results in Table 4, the effects of self-efficacy intensity ( -.070) and self-efficacy generality ( -.179) on near transfer performance were nonsignificant ( p .05), lending no support to Hypothesis 4a. However, the effects of self-efficacy intensity ( .359, p .01) and self-efficacy generality ( .232, p .03) on far transfer performance were statistically significant, supporting Hypothesis 4b.

To test Hypotheses 5a and 5b, which stated that self-efficacy would mediate the relationship between practice variability and transfer performance, it was necessary to establish the conditions of mediation (Baron & Kenny, 1986). The conditions that needed to be met for mediation were (a) practice variability was related to self-efficacy, (b) self-efficacy was related to transfer after accounting for the effects of practice variability, and (c) prac-

tice variability had a nonsignificant effect on transfer after accounting for the effects of self-efficacy. The tests of mediation were conducted for both near (5a) and far (5b) transfer performance, separately.

The first condition, establishing a relationship between practice variability and self-efficacy, was tested in the analyses of Hypotheses 2a and 2b, showing that practice variability was related to self-efficacy generality. The second condition of mediation was tested in the analyses of Hypotheses 4a and 4b, which revealed that self-efficacy intensity and self-efficacy generality were related to far transfer after accounting for the effect of practice variability. However, as self-efficacy intensity was not related to near transfer, the test of mediation for near transfer was not continued. Thus, Hypothesis 5a was not supported.

In the final step, to test self-efficacy generality as a mediator between practice variability and far transfer, a hierarchical regression was conducted predicting far transfer from practice variability (see Table 5). The regression analyses revealed that the effect of practice variability ( .159, p .05) on far transfer performance was nonsignificant. Thus, self-efficacy generality mediated the relationship between practice variability and far transfer, supporting Hypothesis 5b.

The present study examined the role of self-efficacy in explaining the relationship between practice variability and transfer. Although previous studies have demonstrated that self-efficacy intensity (level and strength) can be influenced by some training interventions, the effect of practice variability on each dimension of self-efficacy (intensity and generality) has not been previously examined. Furthermore, previous studies have not examined the role of self-efficacy generality in the transfer process. Specifically, it was proposed that increased practice variability is likely to produce similarity in a person's self-efficacy beliefs across a broader range of a task (generality). This would lead to higher far transfer performance as a person attempts to perform variations of the task not previously taught in training.
Practice variability and self-efficacy. We did not find a relationship between practice variability and the mean of training

performance (Table 1). However, when training performance mean was examined over time or when training performance variability was examined, practice variability did have an impact. Furthermore, practice variability influenced transfer, although the direction was dependent on the type of transfer (i.e., low variability led to higher near transfer, whereas high variability led to higher far transfer; Figure 1). We also found support for the prediction that higher practice variability would lead to higher self-efficacy generality, demonstrating that performing variations of a task resulted in individuals having more similar efficacy beliefs across a wider range of the task. This relationship did not appear to be mediated by performance variability as was expected to be the case. Conversely, neither practice variability nor performance variability influenced self-efficacy intensity.

Self-efficacy and transfer. Although self-efficacy intensity was not related to near transfer, both intensity and generality had independent effects on far transfer. These relationships replicate past research linking self-efficacy with transfer (e.g., Stevens &

Gist, 1997) and extend this research by revealing the role selfefficacy generality plays in transfer. Moreover, they show that having both higher overall self-efficacy intensity and efficacy beliefs that are more closely associated allowed trainees to attempt and succeed at variations of a task that had not been previously taught in training. However, only self-efficacy generality served as an intervening variable between practice variability and far transfer, which highlights the importance of considering this dimension of self-efficacy in the context of practice variability and lays bare the underlying motivational mechanism involved in this transfer process.

It is important to note that we found the dimensions of selfefficacy level and strength to overlap considerably, in fact, forming only one factor. This finding is not surprising given past research that has found level and strength to behave similarly in their relationships with other variables (e.g., performance). Although conceptually these two dimensions may be distinct, from an operational standpoint the measurement of these two dimensions may be redundant (e.g., Cecil & Pinkerton, 2000). In further research, it may make sense to start thinking of the level and strength as together representing an intensity of self-efficacy. Thus, although our original intent was to investigate three dimensions of self-efficacy (level, strength, and generality), the results of our study left our focus on two, intensity and generality. As the dimensions of intensity and generality were found to be unrelated, they may be a more comprehensive representation of the selfefficacy construct.

Future research efforts should focus on examining the antecedents and consequences of self-efficacy generality in order to understand its place in the larger nomological net of motivation and performance constructs. For example, Bandura (e.g., 1997) outlined a number of factors such as vicarious experience and feedback that are likely to influence self-efficacy (level and strength). Furthermore, we did find, consistent with past research (e.g., Martocchio & Judge, 1997), that training performance had a positive relationship with self-efficacy intensity (Table 1), indicating that performance level influences self-efficacy intensity irrespective of the training condition. However, because generality represents an independent dimension of self-efficacy, it is not clear that these factors or antecedents will have similar relationships with it.

In fact, we found that practice variability has distinct effects on these dimensions, and moreover, that there was not a relationship between the training performance level and generality. Consequently, further research is still needed to uncover the exact mechanisms by which practice variability influences self-efficacy generality as well as the boundary conditions of this effect.

Specifically, investigating the mechanism of perceived similarity (e.g., Bong, 1997) could lead to a better understanding of how self-efficacy generality is influenced by practice variability. (Because perceived similarity is independent of the level of feedback, self-efficacy intensity is unlikely to be affected.) For example, practice variability might serve to increase the perceived similarity among task versions and thereby result in higher generality as individuals recognize that past experience is relevant to new versions of the task. To examine this potential relationship, studies could ask participants for their perceptions of the similarity among task versions to determine whether their perceptions of similarity have a bearing on their confidence across the range of tasks. Such research could also serve as a bridge between past and present research by combining motivational (i.e., self-efficacy) and cognitive approaches. That is, from a cognitive approach, the information-processing perspective suggests that exposing people to several versions of a stimulus will help them integrate the information into a common representation in memory (Baldwin & Ford, 1988), possibly aided by the increase in perceived similarity among stimuli. Finally, studying this mechanism could serve as a manipulation check to ensure that participants perceive variability, which was lacking in the present study.

Another avenue for future research concerns the issue of variability. That is, practice variability can be operationalized in a number of ways within the same task. For example, training on using computers can be varied by changing the program used, type of computer, and number of functions and features available to the user, among others. One limitation of the current study is that variability was operationalized by varying only one dimension. Theoretically, one would expect that self-efficacy generality would follow along the same dimension that was used to operationalize variability. For example, we found that varying the number of attributes that was changing was related to self-efficacy generality along that dimension. We would not expect, on the other hand, that trainees would show an equal amount of generality for performing this task that varied along other dimensions such as the cover story

of the decision-making task (e.g., stock market simulation vs. military), type of input device (keyboard, mouse, and so forth.), or type of decision to be made. However, future research is needed to establish the exact nature of the relationship between variability along various task dimensions, self-efficacy generality, and transfer. Research along these lines would also allow for stronger tests of near versus far transfer.

Although the focus of the present research was to investigate the relationship among practice variability, self-efficacy, and transfer in isolation, future research could address this relationship through an attribute–treatment interaction perspective. Although the relationships were not hypothesized, we conducted some exploratory analyses with cognitive ability and dispositional traits (i.e., goal orientation) as moderators of the practice variability effect. Similar to Gully, Payne, Koles, and Whiteman (2002), we found a significant interaction between cognitive ability and training condition on (far transfer) performance ( -1.57, p .02). We found that in the constant practice condition, the difference between low cognitive ability individuals and high cognitive ability individuals was accentuated on the far transfer task, with low cognitive ability individuals performing lower. Although the level of far transfer performance did not differ for high-cognitive-ability individuals as a result of training condition, the variable condition did result in the low-cognitive-ability individuals performing at a level similar to high-cognitive-ability individuals. Although this finding was the only significant aptitude–treatment interaction, it does provide some initial support for integrating the examination of individual differences into the current model of research.

Finally, although the present study was conducted in a lab with college students, past research has shown that lab- and field-based findings correspond across a wide variety of domains (Anderson, Lindsay, & Bushman, 1999) with both student and adult populations (Dipboye & Flanagan, 1979). However, future research should replicate these findings in the field with an organizational sample, in which incumbents may be expected to perform tasks requiring similar capabilities. For example, in the physical ability realm, a firefighter is expected to enter buildings using various tools of different sizes and weights, for example, a pry bar versus an ax (Blakley, Quin˜ones, Crawford, & Jago, 1994). A training program using variable practice could enhance self-efficacy generality for and lead to greater transfer from different types of tools. The extension of this research into the field would allow for both evidence from a working sample as well as evidence within the physical ability realm. Thus, although this study provides initial evidence for the role of self-efficacy generality in the transfer process, more research is needed to further examine the relationship between practice variability and transfer.
